messages.author: 44f1f9ea3d910e12
messages.subject: Left truncation and esw
parts:
Hi listfolk,

 

I was trying to figure out what the mrds package in R actually returns when estimating esw with left truncation, and maybe someone can check if I’m right here:

 

I used binned observations from aerial surveys, with a 44m ‘blind’area below the aircraft, so I tried left truncation with left=44. To cross-check the results, I also tried substracting 44m from all data, so I have the same transect/bin width but no left truncation.

Now to my surprise esw was wider (by app. 20m) for the non-truncated data.

 

From this I conclude that in the case of left truncation, esw seems to be measured from the truncation distance ‘left’ rather than from the transect line. This makes sense, but I wouldn’t have guessed from the documentation of the mrds package.

 

While the precision of my esw estimates may be limited for the present data set, I still wonder which of the two approaches is the more reliable?

 

Best wishes

Jochen

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Left truncation and esw
parts:
Jochen

This is a topic that has come up several times on the list; not specifically in the context of the mrds package, but about aerial surveys in general.  The issue is less about the effective strip with than about the fitting of the detection function and subsequent estimation of density or abundance.

You ask which of the two approaches to employ.  Here is a reply from Len Thomas dated 14June2004

Having left truncated, you have two options: (1) fit a detection function to the truncated data as is.  This does not assume that g(x)=1 at the truncation point. (2) subtract the truncation distance from all data -- effectively move the centreline out to be at the truncation distance.  This then assumes that g(x)=1 at the truncation distance.  The former strategy has a weaker assumption, but will give higher variance as the detection function close to the line has no data to tell it where to fit -- it will be relying on the data from > the left truncation point and the assumed shape of the detection function.

For a non-aerial survey perceptive, have a look at Buckland et al. (2001) section 8.4.3.  There you will find a discussion of terrestrial nest data for pintail ducks, where the data were analysed in the two ways you describe, resulting in these two figures:
